problem_context: Current generative modeling approaches face fundamental challenges in mapping from one distribution to another. While discriminative models simply map individual samples to labels, generative models must learn mappings between entire distributions - a significantly more complex task. Existing approaches often require iterative procedures at inference time, involving multiple network evaluations to progressively transform samples from noise to data. This creates computational inefficiency and complexity. There is a need for generative modeling approaches that can produce high-quality samples in a single forward pass, without requiring iterative refinement procedures during generation. A key insight is that neural network training itself is inherently iterative - could this iterative nature of training be leveraged to evolve distributions, rather than requiring iteration at inference time?
desirable_properties: Should perform generation in a single forward pass without iterative refinement
Should achieve competitive sample quality compared to multi-step methods
Should work across different data modalities and domains
Should scale effectively to high-resolution data
Should avoid mode collapse and capture the full data distribution
Should support conditional generation with flexible conditioning
Should not require adversarial training or unstable optimization procedures
Should leverage the inherent iterative nature of neural network training to evolve the generated distribution
Should define some form of equilibrium condition where the evolution naturally stops when the target is reached
field_context: This work addresses fundamental challenges in generative modeling, where the goal is to learn mappings between probability distributions. The field has seen various paradigms including iterative refinement methods, adversarial approaches, and likelihood-based models, each with their own trade-offs between sample quality, computational efficiency, and training stability. A conceptual shift might involve thinking about how distributions evolve during the training process itself, rather than just at inference time.
